question: Isn't the term "Sunni Islam" divisive? Why not just say Islam and Muslims?
asked: You have used this term, Sunni Islam, many times in your lectures. Don't you think this term is divisive? Why don't we just say Islam or Muslims? Why do you use the term Sunni?
answer:
This is a very valid question. A lot of people ask this question often, and they are inshallah very well intentioned. They want to bring about unity in the ummah, and they feel, why do we have to have all of these divisions?

I say, I sympathize with your sentiment, but whether I use the term or not, these divisions exist in the ummah, and my usage or non-usage will not change the fact that different Muslims have different understandings of Islam. So we are not using the term Sunni as a proper noun; we're using it as an adjective. We have one proper noun. Allah says in the Qur'an, He is the one that has called you Muslims, before, from the time of Ibrahim, and now in the time of Muhammad ﷺ. The name that we have as a religion is Islam. We are Muslims.

Now, within Islam, we would like there to be one interpretation, and the correct interpretation. But from the time of the Sahaba, differences occurred. The first splinter movement to break away and have a different understanding of Islam was the group that is now called the Kharijites. But they weren't called Kharijites back then; at that time they were called the Haruriyya. So they had a different understanding of Islam, and they said, for example, that we will not accept the Sunnah, we're only going to accept the Qur'an. This was one of their main points.

So for example, when Allah says in the Qur'an, "The thief, cut off his hand," the Sunnah tells us that the hand, when all the conditions are met, is cut off at the wrist. But the Arabic word yad means anything. So when someone stole, the Kharijites would cut off the hand from here, because the Qur'an says cut off the limb, al-yad, and in Arabic yad can be anything. So because they didn't take the Sunnah as their source, they had a very different understanding of the Shari'ah. Because they said, we're not going to accept hadith. Generally they rejected hadith. That was the Khawarij of old.

So the point being, this splinter occurred in the time of the late Sahaba, after the assassination of Ali, as you are aware; that's the whole issue that happened. As well, in the time of the late Sahaba, other deviations began: to reject Qadr. The Qadariyyah they were called. They rejected Qadr. They said there's no such thing as predestination, we don't believe in Qadr. So they were called the Qadariyyah, the deniers of Qadr. And another group came along and they said, actions are not a part of iman; we will delay our affairs to Allah. So they were called the delayers, the Murji'ah. This is also in the late Sahaba time.

And then the difference between the Sunni and the Shia came along. This came along after Karbala, so none of the Sahaba were really involved in that, but in the time of the tabi'un it came along. They called themselves Shi'at Ali, the supporters of Ali, and then "Ali" was dropped and now they call themselves Shia.

So the point being that these terms have existed from the time of the Sahaba and the tabi'un, and we have to somehow characterize. Whether you like it or not, there are different understandings of Islam. So what do we do? How do I explain? You can say, "according to those who accept the Sunnah, and respect the Sahaba, and affirm Qadr," and you list all of the points of Sunni Islam, or you can say, "according to Sunni Islam." Which of the two? Number one or number two?

The term itself: where do we get it from? It is a term that is found in the Sunnah itself. It's not something that is invented by outsiders. And that is why the first person to use this term, that we know for sure, as a full term, is none other than Ibn Abbas. On the verse in the Qur'an, "On that day, certain faces will be bright, certain faces will be cloudy," Ibn Abbas said: the people of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah, their faces will be bright, and the people who rejected the Sunnah and fell into deviation... He meant the Khawarij, because at that time the Khawarij were a fanatical group. They were murderers and killers.

And again, later on we'll have longer lectures, but I have said this bluntly and I stand by this: if you study Khariji history, ISIS is a manifestation of Kharijism. This is what the Khawarij were: killing Muslims, everybody is a kafir unless you're with our interpretation. My way, or not just the highway, but the grave. My way or we will kill you. And they kill more Muslims than... And the same fanaticism that we find in these groups goes back, as our Prophet ﷺ said: there will always be this group, the Khawarij, they will always be coming out, back and forth, until Dajjal comes. And in one hadith he said, and they will then fight on the side of Dajjal.

Pause here, footnote. We see, a'udhu billah, a'udhu billah, evil scholars in our time still justifying tyranny and whatnot, on the side of the taghuts of our time. Don't be surprised that you're going to find them on the side of Dajjal himself when that happens. We ask Allah for 'afiyah.

The point being that the term Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah, where did it come from? Ibn Abbas. Where did Ibn Abbas get it? Do you think he pulled it out of his pocket? He turned his kufi, his turban, upside down and pulled it out? Not out of his hat, but out of his turban. Where did he get it from? It is found in the hadith itself.

Our Prophet ﷺ said, "You will see a lot of ikhtilaf after I die. You will see a lot of ikhtilaf after I die." This hadith is in Abu Dawud: "Then I command you to follow my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided khulafa." In another hadith, reported in Tirmidhi, our Prophet ﷺ said that my ummah will divide into many groups, 73 he said. They said, "Ya Rasulullah, which one should we follow?" He said, "Al-Jama'ah. Follow the Jama'ah."

What does the Jama'ah mean? It has many meanings. Number one, and this is the primary meaning of Jama'ah: the bulk of the ummah. Follow them; follow the bulk of the ummah. Al-Jama'ah means the group; follow the group. Number two, Jama'ah means the Sahaba. The main Jama'ah is the Sahaba; follow the Sahaba. And there are other interpretations as well. The point being, in this hadith he said follow the Jama'ah, and in the other hadith he said follow the Sunnah. So we take this hadith, we take that hadith, and we get the term what? The people of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah. We got it straight from the hadith.

And subhanAllah, from the earliest of Islam, the main splinter groups that formed, they rejected hadith. The Khawarij rejected hadith, the Murji'ah rejected hadith, the Qadariyyah rejected hadith. And then those who supported Ali, or we should say, they claimed to support Ali. In my more academic, detailed lecture that I give online, you will find it. I say, in reality, we are the true supporters of Ali. We are the real supporters of Ali. That group is saying they are supporters; they are not the real supporters of Ali radiyallahu 'anhu.

But the point being, those who claim to be on the side of Ali, the partisans of Ali, they don't follow the Sunnah, do they? Their second source is what the imams say. For us, what is our source? The Qur'an and the Sunnah. For them, what is their source? The Qur'an and the imams. So we have a fundamental difference, and that difference is what? Sunnah. So the main point of difference with our interpretation of Islam is that for us the Sunnah is a necessary source. You cannot understand the Qur'an without the Sunnah. So we call ourselves Sunni.

Now, I understand an innocent Muslim says, oh, we are using this term to be divisive. And you know what, at a certain level I agree with you. But it is possible for a correct Qur'anic term to be misapplied and used to divide the ummah. So then what do you think about a term that is not in the Qur'an? It can be misused and misapplied. The fact that the term can be misused does not negate the validity of the term.

For example, in the Qur'an we have the terms muhajir and ansar. Correct? It's in the Qur'an, very explicit in the Qur'an. Allah 'azza wa jall mentions:

> وَالْمُهَاجِرِينَ وَالْأَنصَارِ

These are Qur'anic terms, yes or no? Allah divided the Muslims into muhajir and ansar, yes or no? Okay.

What happened on the return from the Ghazwa of Banu al-Mustaliq? The munafiqun began irritating, and they said:

> لَئِن رَّجَعْنَا إِلَى الْمَدِينَةِ لَيُخْرِجَنَّ الْأَعَزُّ مِنْهَا الْأَذَلَّ

And they began causing discord, and they engineered something and whatnot; it's a long story. And the muhajirun and the ansar, two of their youth started fighting, one an Ansari and one a Muhajir, and one of them beat up the other. Which is what happens amongst teenagers and kids; you have to deal with it. This is testosterone coming out; you have to calm them down. That's the problem of our youth. This is common.

So we calm them down and they calm down. But they didn't calm down. Each one said, he did this, how dare he! And anger inflamed, and the voice went out: "Muhajirun, come! Ansar, come!" And they lined up to have a fist fight amongst themselves. The Prophet ﷺ heard the commotion and he came out, and his face was angry, like a pomegranate. This was the highest form of anger, where they say his face was angry. And he said, "While I am still alive, while I am still alive, you are doing this?" And he rebuked them, a harsh rebuke, and he calmed them down, and he said, leave this division; it is something that goes back to jahiliyyah.

Now, the terms muhajir and ansar, correct or incorrect? What happened here, was it used correctly? No. Do we negate muhajir and ansar because it was used incorrectly? No, we simply use it correctly. Are there fanatics that use the term to inspire hatred? Wallahi, yes there are. We correct that hatred. The term is not meant to inspire hatred. The term is not meant to make people uncomfortable or make them feel anything like that. The term is meant as a description; we are describing.

When you ask me a question sometimes about advanced theology, I have to say, well, we Sunnis believe this, so that you know that there are other interpretations. I obviously don't agree with those interpretations, but you know what, it is necessary to be educated. It's necessary to know what is the red line. Very necessary.

And I will be very frank amongst you and say: just because somebody disagrees doesn't make them a kafir. This is a very important point. Because the rest of the groups... We said it many weeks ago, three, four, five weeks ago, I forget now, we talked about the 73 groups. I said these groups are all Muslim groups. We're not talking about the groups outside of Islam. Those that the Prophet ﷺ said are incorrect, misguided, he called them "my ummah": my ummah will divide into 73. These aren't the kafirs. There are groups that are outside the fold of Islam; they are not within Islam. And I gave an example: any group that says there's a messenger after the Nabi ﷺ, they're not within Islam; they're not from the 73. So the 73 are within Islam.

So it is important we educate ourselves, not so that we agree, but:

1. So that we know our faith.
2. If the opportunity arises, we call them to the truth.
3. So that we at least create a civil society.

You will hear from me very often: listen, we need to learn to disagree without being angry or violent. What good does it do? Wallahi, my dear Muslim brothers and sisters, look back home, the violence that takes place between the sects of Islam. Look back home: the anger, the fanaticism. This is not from the Sunnah. It is not from the Sahaba themselves.

And I'll give you the best example for this: the Khawarij, the ones who became so fanatical, the ones who became so crazed, and they started killing people and whatnot. Before, they were only talking; they weren't acting that fanatical. Ali radiyallahu 'anhu sent Ibn Abbas to debate with them, and they had a big debate. A third of them came back to the truth and two-thirds remained as they were, or it is said one-third remained and two-thirds came back; both riwayat are found. Basically, a large amount remained, over two, three thousand people remained Kharijites. They refused to change their 'aqidah.

Now, this isn't an un-Islamic state. This is the Khulafa al-Rashidun. This isn't just a khalifa of the Umayyads or Abbasids or Mamluks or Mughals. This is Ali ibn Abi Talib radiyallahu 'anhu. Four thousand Muslims say, we don't agree with your theology, we're not going to be Sunni. Ali radiyallahu 'anhu said, there's nothing we can do. I cannot force you to believe like I believe. I can't open your heart and force you to be Sunni. I cannot force you. You go, you live your lives, you do as you want. He gave them freedom of interpretation, in an ideal Islamic state.

What do you think, in the modern countries we cannot give them freedom of interpretation? Wallahi, think about it. In an ideal Islamic state, under the Khulafa al-Rashidun, Ali radiyallahu 'anhu said to them, you are free to do as you please; we can't do anything other than talk to you. But don't harm the believers. Don't harm the believers.

The Khawarij, they didn't stop at talking. They began to attack, hijack, and then, what was the last straw? They massacred brutally Muhammad ibn Ammar ibn Yasir, Ammar ibn Yasir's son, and they took his wife, who was pregnant, a'udhu billah, slit her throat open, not through the belly. Just gruesome. Fanatics. As you see these people burning in cages and massacring, it's the exact same mentality, thinking that they're defending Islam. This is their fanaticism. Same thing.

So Ali radiyallahu 'anhu couldn't let that go: you're disturbing civil order. So he fought them. But before that, what did he say? We have no right over you as long as you don't harm us. SubhanAllah. If this is in an ideal Islamic land, I mean, can you go and force people to accept your interpretation? As long as they're not violent, you have the right to debate, you have the right to argue, you have the right to preach the truth. But if a group of people insist, we're not going to accept your theology, what are you going to do?

**So the term Sunni is not meant to divide. It is meant merely to educate and to preach.** Some people misuse it, agreed. Some people incite violence and hatred, agreed. We need to talk to them, and we need to make sure they don't do that. It doesn't negate the validity of the term.
